newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Cambodia ASEAN membership still on hold.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia ASEAN membership still on hold.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Wednesday reaffirmed its decision to put Cambodia's membership on hold, Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi said.
He told a news conference after a luncheon meeting of the seven ASEAN foreign ministers that Cambodia could not join the regional grouping while there was still political instability in the country.

"We feel there is still instability in Cambodia, and we reaffirmed our decision (of July 10) not to induct Cambodia on the 23rd," Abdullah said. He added there was no change to Cambodia's status as an observer to ASEAN.
ASEAN had grouped Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. On Wednesday, it admitted Burma and Laos as full members.
ASEAN's decision came despite a last-minute plea by Cambodia to be accepted as a member, and a softening of its stance toward the group's mediation efforts.

Cambodia was thrown into turmoil when Second Prime Minister Hun Sen earlier this month overthrew First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh after two days of intense fighting in the capital Phnom Penh.
Hun Sen has backed Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot to replace Ranariddh.
Adbullah indicated that the nomination was in question. "The position of prime minister still remains unresolved," he said.
"At the moment, as far as we are concerned, Prince (Norodom) Ranariddh is still first prime minister, and no new prime minister is coming up," he said.
Ranariddh, now in exile, is expected to arrive in Jakarta later on Wednesday from Singapore, where he met Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong.
The ousted premier is trying to garner support from regional leaders.
Indonesia was one of the co-chairmen of the 1991 Paris peace talks that ended years of bloodshed in Cambodia and laid the groundwork for United Nations-sponsored elections in Cambodia in 1993.

At a meeting earlier on Wednesday, ASEAN's foreign ministers received a report from a team comprising the foreign ministers of Thailand, the Philippines and Indonesia that had met Hun Sen, Ranariddh and King Norodom Sihanouk.
The mission's mediation efforts were initially rebuffed by Hun Sen, who told foreigners not to interfere, but Ung Huot on Wednesday said his country welcomed ASEAN's help.
Meanwhile, President Clinton's special envoy on Cambodia, Stephen Solarz, said on Wednesday he wanted to work with ASEAN on a solution to Phnom Penh's troubles.

"We think the best chance of achieving an acceptable resolution is if we can find a way to work together," said Solarz, who is on an Asian diplomatic shuttle seeking a solution to the turmoil in Cambodia.
